subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Reference Class Forecasting
description: A fast breakdown of Reference Class Forecasting for builders.

hook.text: Your home renovation budget is $50,000. History says similar projects average $75,000. Trust history.

buildup.text: Kahneman calls this the 'outside view.' Instead of planning from your case, check what usually happens.

discovery.text: Reference class forecasting: compare your project to similar past projects instead of trusting your gut.

twist.text: The inside view feels more accurate because it uses your unique details. But it's systematically too optimistic.

climax.text: Find your reference class first. What's the average outcome? Start there, then adjust for specifics.

punchline.text: Your project isn't as unique as you think.

quiz.question: What does reference class forecasting recommend?
options: Compare your project to similar past projects
Ignore historical data and focus on details

details.summary: Reference class forecasting combats the planning fallacy by estimating outcomes based on the statistical distribution of similar past projects rather than the inside view of the specific project. It moves prediction from optimistic imagination to empirical base rates.
details.whyItMatters: Ninety percent of major projects exceed their budgets and timelines. Reference class forecasting corrects this by forcing planners to consider how similar projects actually turned out, rather than believing their project is uniquely different.
takeaways: Base predictions on how similar past projects actually performed
Reference class forecasting corrects the planning fallacy systematically
Inside views are optimistic; outside views are more accurate

faq.question: How do you apply reference class forecasting?
faq.answer: Identify a class of similar past projects, gather their actual outcomes, and use the resulting distribution as your baseline prediction. Adjust only modestly for unique factors. This disciplined approach produces dramatically more accurate forecasts.

faq.question: Why don't more organizations use reference class forecasting?
faq.answer: Because optimistic inside-view projections are more psychologically appealing and politically convenient. Telling stakeholders that similar projects ran 50 percent over budget is less popular than promising this one will be different.
